summary.html:
Overview

  • Speaker: Gil Feig
  • Channel: AI Engineer
  • Main topic: Enterprise AI infrastructure and the necessity of context graphs for production AI applications
  • Purpose: To explain what a context graph is, why companies need one beyond simple MCP servers or live API lookups, and how to architect and build a robust, traceable context layer for enterprise AI agents. Gil Feig, co-founder and CTO of Merge, explains why companies need a context graph to power production AI applications effectively. He breaks down the components of a company context graph, including third-party data, structured context, memories, and skills. He outlines the tiers of context—prompt/skills/memory, live API calls, cached data, and derived context—and discusses selection strategies, syncing layers, routing, and provenance requirements for reliable enterprise AI systems.

Topic Map

Introduction to Merge and Context Graphs

  • Explanation: Gil Feig introduces Merge, a connective infrastructure platform for production AI, and sets the agenda for discussing why companies need a context graph and how to build one.
  • Key claims:
    • Merge provides unified, agent handler, and gateway infrastructure for enterprise AI.
    • Simple MCP server connections are not enough for complex semantic queries across large company data sets.
  • Examples:
    • Connecting to Zendesk or Salesforce.
  • Terminology:
    • Merge
    • context graph
    • MCP server
    • agent handler
    • gateway
  • Why it matters: Establishes the foundational need for robust enterprise AI infrastructure beyond simple API wrappers.

What is a Context Graph

  • Explanation: Defines the company context graph as the company's brain, encompassing third-party data, structured context, memories, and skills rather than literal node-and-edge graph databases.
  • Key claims:
    • A context graph consists of third-party data, structured context, memories, and skills.
    • Skills are a vital part of a context graph.
  • Examples:
    • Using NetSuite, Jira, and static documents as data sources.
  • Terminology:
    • third-party data
    • structured context
    • memories
    • skills
  • Why it matters: Provides a mental model for how AI agents ingest and process organizational knowledge.

The Limitations of Live Lookups and MCP

  • Explanation: Demonstrates through an example why live API lookups (like querying Zendesk for customer tickets one by one) fail when scaling to broader questions like finding all upset customers over a year.
  • Key claims:
    • Live lookup methodology in platforms like MCP does not support live aggregation across vast datasets.
    • Platforms do not incentivize vectorizing data due to cost and maintenance.
  • Examples:
    • Asking 'Why was customer A upset last week?' vs 'Which customers were upset last week?'
  • Terminology:
    • MCP
    • live lookup
    • vectorization
    • API sync
  • Why it matters: Highlights why a syncing layer and local cache/vector database are required alongside live tools.

Different Tiers of Context

  • Explanation: Categorizes context into four distinct tiers: Prompt, skills, and memory; Live API calls; Cached data; and Derived context.
  • Key claims:
    • Live API calls are cheaper and easier to build for simple lookups.
    • Cached data is essential for complex semantic queries but requires syncing and vectorization.
    • Derived context involves precomputed summaries and embeddings for faster retrieval.
  • Examples:
    • Account Summary cache refreshed every 15 minutes vs live CRM calls.
  • Terminology:
    • prompt skills and memory
    • live API calls
    • cached data
    • derived context
  • Why it matters: Helps architects choose the right storage and retrieval strategy for different types of agent queries.

Context Selection Strategy and Flow

  • Explanation: Explains the decision tree for handling user prompts: checking skills/memory first, then cached data freshness, falling back to live APIs when necessary.
  • Key claims:
    • Agents should check skills and memory before querying live or cached layers.
    • Caching data reduces timeout risks during large dataset lookups.
  • Examples:
    • Checking skills for customer happiness policies before querying survey data.
  • Terminology:
    • skill match
    • cache freshness
    • live API fallback
    • router
    • summarizer
  • Why it matters: Ensures agents efficiently route queries to the most appropriate context source.

Traceability and Provenance

  • Explanation: Emphasizes the importance of knowing where data came from, who requested it, when it was fetched, and what rules invalidate it for auditing and debugging.
  • Key claims:
    • Every context node passed to a model must be traceable.
    • Provenance is critical for business-critical decisions and versioning.
  • Examples:
    • Tracing a summary back to source ticket IDs and fetch timestamps.
  • Terminology:
    • traceability
    • provenance
    • metadata
    • invalidation
    • versioning
  • Why it matters: Prevents blind reliance on stale or unverified data in automated enterprise decisions.

Key Points

Tools are not enough for context

  • Explanation: Connecting an agent to MCP servers or APIs is insufficient for complex enterprise reasoning; organizations need a structured context graph.
  • Evidence: Live lookup pagination and timeouts when searching thousands of tickets.
  • Practical implication: Architects must implement a syncing and caching layer alongside live tool calls.

More data is not always better

  • Explanation: Pulling massive amounts of raw context causes context window overload and timeouts. Quality and freshness matter more than volume.
  • Evidence: Pulling 5 tickets instead of full history to avoid API timeouts.
  • Practical implication: Use derived summaries and targeted caching strategies.

Traceability is mandatory for enterprise AI

  • Explanation: Models must provide provenance for every piece of data used in decision-making to enable auditing and debugging.
  • Evidence: Citations and source links in chat interfaces.
  • Practical implication: Store metadata, fetch timestamps, scope permissions, and invalidation rules with every context node.

Frameworks, Models & Processes

Context Tier Architecture

  • How it works: Categorizes enterprise knowledge into layers based on access speed, cost, and complexity.
  • Components:
    • Prompt, skills, and memory
    • Live API calls
    • Cached data
    • Derived context
  • When to use: When designing enterprise AI agent architectures that require both real-time actions and historical reasoning.

Context Selection Flow

  • How it works: A decision tree for routing prompts through skills, memory, cache checks, and live API fallbacks.
  • Components:
    • Query received
    • Skill/memory match check
    • Cache freshness check
    • Live API fallback
    • Summarization and generation
  • When to use: When implementing agentic routing and tool execution logic.

Examples & Case Studies

Asking an agent why customer A was upset last week using a single Zendesk tool call.

  • Illustrates: The sufficiency of live API lookups for simple, scoped queries.
  • Lesson: Live tool calls work well when the data scope is narrow.

Asking an agent which customers were upset over the last year.

  • Illustrates: The failure of live lookups due to pagination limits and timeouts.
  • Lesson: Complex semantic queries require a synced local cache and vector database.

Checking account summary cache freshness before calling the CRM API.

  • Illustrates: Optimizing context selection using tiered storage.
  • Lesson: Use cached data when fresh enough; fall back to live APIs only when necessary.

Actionable Takeaways

  • Immediate:
    • Audit your agent context sources and identify what requires local syncing vs live API calls.
    • Implement metadata tracking for data provenance on all ingested context nodes.
  • Strategic:
    • Build a multi-tiered context strategy combining prompts, memory, cached vector stores, and live tools.
    • Treat context selection and routing as core enterprise business logic.
  • Questions to investigate:
    • How do we handle cache invalidation for rapidly changing enterprise data sources?
    • What is the cost tradeoff between vectorizing enterprise databases versus making live API calls?

Claims Worth Verifying

  • No enterprise platforms incentivize vectorizing data because of cost and maintenance. (industry observation)
  • Live lookup methodologies in platforms like MCP do not support live aggregation across vast datasets. (architectural claim)

Notable Quotes

"Why your company needs a context graph and how to build it" (at 0:30) "Tools aren't context" (at 22:13)

Compressed Summary

  • Context graphs encompass third-party data, structured context, memories, and skills.
  • Context tiers include prompts/skills/memory, live API calls, cached data, and derived context.
  • Traceability and provenance are essential for auditing enterprise AI decisions.
  • Keywords: context graph, ai agents, caching, provenance, mcp
  • Core insight: Enterprise AI requires more than live tool calls; it needs a structured, multi-tiered context graph with syncing, caching, and strict data provenance.

  - Live lookup methodology in platforms like MCP does not support live aggregation across vast datasets.
  - Platforms do not incentivize vectorizing data due to cost and maintenance.
- **Examples**:
  - Asking 'Why was customer A upset last week?' vs 'Which customers were upset last week?'
- **Terminology**:
  - MCP
  - live lookup
  - vectorization
  - API sync
- **Why it matters**: Highlights why a syncing layer and local cache/vector database are required alongside live tools.
### Different Tiers of Context
- **Explanation**: Categorizes context into four distinct tiers: Prompt, skills, and memory; Live API calls; Cached data; and Derived context.
- **Key claims**:
  - Live API calls are cheaper and easier to build for simple lookups.
  - Cached data is essential for complex semantic queries but requires syncing and vectorization.
  - Derived context involves precomputed summaries and embeddings for faster retrieval.
- **Examples**:
  - Account Summary cache refreshed every 15 minutes vs live CRM calls.
- **Terminology**:
  - prompt skills and memory
  - live API calls
  - cached data
  - derived context
- **Why it matters**: Helps architects choose the right storage and retrieval strategy for different types of agent queries.
### Context Selection Strategy and Flow
- **Explanation**: Explains the decision tree for handling user prompts: checking skills/memory first, then cached data freshness, falling back to live APIs when necessary.
- **Key claims**:
  - Agents should check skills and memory before querying live or cached layers.
  - Caching data reduces timeout risks during large dataset lookups.
- **Examples**:
  - Checking skills for customer happiness policies before querying survey data.
- **Terminology**:
  - skill match
  - cache freshness
  - live API fallback
  - router
  - summarizer
- **Why it matters**: Ensures agents efficiently route queries to the most appropriate context source.
### Traceability and Provenance
- **Explanation**: Emphasizes the importance of knowing where data came from, who requested it, when it was fetched, and what rules invalidate it for auditing and debugging.
- **Key claims**:
  - Every context node passed to a model must be traceable.
  - Provenance is critical for business-critical decisions and versioning.
- **Examples**:
  - Tracing a summary back to source ticket IDs and fetch timestamps.
- **Terminology**:
  - traceability
  - provenance
  - metadata
  - invalidation
  - versioning
- **Why it matters**: Prevents blind reliance on stale or unverified data in automated enterprise decisions.
## Key Points
### Tools are not enough for context
- **Explanation**: Connecting an agent to MCP servers or APIs is insufficient for complex enterprise reasoning; organizations need a structured context graph.
- **Evidence**: Live lookup pagination and timeouts when searching thousands of tickets.
- **Practical implication**: Architects must implement a syncing and caching layer alongside live tool calls.
### More data is not always better
- **Explanation**: Pulling massive amounts of raw context causes context window overload and timeouts. Quality and freshness matter more than volume.
- **Evidence**: Pulling 5 tickets instead of full history to avoid API timeouts.
- **Practical implication**: Use derived summaries and targeted caching strategies.
### Traceability is mandatory for enterprise AI
- **Explanation**: Models must provide provenance for every piece of data used in decision-making to enable auditing and debugging.
- **Evidence**: Citations and source links in chat interfaces.
- **Practical implication**: Store metadata, fetch timestamps, scope permissions, and invalidation rules with every context node.
## Frameworks, Models & Processes
### Context Tier Architecture
- **How it works**: Categorizes enterprise knowledge into layers based on access speed, cost, and complexity.
- **Components**:
  - Prompt, skills, and memory
  - Live API calls
  - Cached data
  - Derived context
- **When to use**: When designing enterprise AI agent architectures that require both real-time actions and historical reasoning.
### Context Selection Flow
- **How it works**: A decision tree for routing prompts through skills, memory, cache checks, and live API fallbacks.
- **Components**:
  - Query received
  - Skill/memory match check
  - Cache freshness check
  - Live API fallback
  - Summarization and generation
- **When to use**: When implementing agentic routing and tool execution logic.
## Examples & Case Studies
### Asking an agent why customer A was upset last week using a single Zendesk tool call.
- **Illustrates**: The sufficiency of live API lookups for simple, scoped queries.
- **Lesson**: Live tool calls work well when the data scope is narrow.
### Asking an agent which customers were upset over the last year.
- **Illustrates**: The failure of live lookups due to pagination limits and timeouts.
- **Lesson**: Complex semantic queries require a synced local cache and vector database.
### Checking account summary cache freshness before calling the CRM API.
- **Illustrates**: Optimizing context selection using tiered storage.
- **Lesson**: Use cached data when fresh enough; fall back to live APIs only when necessary.
## Actionable Takeaways
- **Immediate**:
  - Audit your agent context sources and identify what requires local syncing vs live API calls.
  - Implement metadata tracking for data provenance on all ingested context nodes.
- **Strategic**:
  - Build a multi-tiered context strategy combining prompts, memory, cached vector stores, and live tools.
  - Treat context selection and routing as core enterprise business logic.
- **Questions to investigate**:
  - How do we handle cache invalidation for rapidly changing enterprise data sources?
  - What is the cost tradeoff between vectorizing enterprise databases versus making live API calls?
## Claims Worth Verifying
- No enterprise platforms incentivize vectorizing data because of cost and maintenance. (industry observation)
- Live lookup methodologies in platforms like MCP do not support live aggregation across vast datasets. (architectural claim)
